newsitem.title: UK: British Airways strike grounds planes.
newsitem.headline: British Airways strike grounds planes.

text.p: British Airways was hit by a debilitating strike on Wednesday when cabin crew launched a three-day stoppage that left thousands of passengers stranded.
With just 20 percent of flights operating, British Airways put on a brave face and said many planes would still fly even as its Heathrow hub faced huge disruption.

"On a normal day, we would expect to carry 40,000 passengers out of Heathrow. The number carried today will be about 14,000, which is about 35 percent of the usual numbers," said BA spokeswoman Terri Urquhart.

Members of the Transport and General Workers' Union began the strike at 6.00 a.m. (0500 GMT) despite a warning that strikers would lose perks and face a lockout unless they promised to work normally in the future.
BA, which operates 1,000 flights a day worldwide, said 135 flights -- 69 percent of its schedule -- from Heathrow, west of London, were grounded.
"But it's changing by the moment as crew report or not, as the case might be," said Urquhart.
"Yesterday about 350 crew reported sick, which was obviously an indication of what's happening. I suspect there will be more sicknesses today," she said.
She said four-fifth of all BA flights, when small island hoppers were included, would not take off.
Pickets carrying banners gathered in the early morning sun near BA's headquarters at Heathrow, while usually frenetic Terminal One was eerily quiet.
As for a breakthrough, both sides expressed hope of a deal, though not in time to stop this stoppage.
At the heart of the dispute are plans by BA to save 42 million pounds ($70.7 million) from cabin crew operations. The unions are threatening further 72-hour strikes.
As the strike began, TGWU negotiator George Ryde said a new confrontation could be averted.
"If we got proper negotiations underway with an objective to secure an agreement, it would avoid any further industrial action," he told BBC television.
He said the issue was not the amount of money under discussion, but how it was to be saved.
"We all know change has to come. We'll find the 42 million (pounds) but not the way in which British Airways wants to do it," he said.
British Airways said it was "delighted" the unions were prepared to meet its cost targets but had not seen such proposals at the negotiating table.
"As yet, no sign of any movement," said Urquhart.

British travel agents have been flooded with calls from customers trying to find alternative flights and BA said its contingency plan, aimed at keeping as many flights running as possible, would swing into action.

Urquhart said the timing of the strike was unfortunate -- the airline last month carried out an expensive facelift aimed at renewing its image -- but that the key to preserving the company's good name was in how it handled the crisis.
"It's obviously upsetting to passengers," she said. "This is disappointing and I think a lot of it depends on how we recover the situation. That's our main focus at the moment."
